notes.meaning: Jesus continued teaching the crowds and leaders using parables, which are short stories that teach a spiritual lesson. Even though his enemies had fallen silent, Jesus knew what they were thinking in their hearts. He used these stories to explain what the kingdom of God is like and what happens when people reject it.

God is pictured here as a king who arranged a great wedding celebration for his Son, Jesus. In the Bible, God's close love for his people is often compared to a marriage. This royal feast represents all the rich spiritual blessings and joy that God provides in salvation.

The king sent his servants to tell the invited guests that the celebration had begun, but they refused to come. In history, God first gave this invitation to the Jewish people through the ancient prophets. Turning down a king's banquet made no sense, showing that sinners stay away from God simply because they refuse his goodness.

The king patiently sent more servants to describe the wonderful feast, explaining that the choice meats were cooked and everything was ready. This points to the apostles preaching the good news after Jesus died and rose again. God prepares the entire meal of salvation for us, and we are invited simply to come and receive it.

Some of the guests completely ignored the message and went off to their own fields and businesses. They cared far more about making money and keeping up daily routines than attending the king's feast. Ordinary work is good, but it becomes harmful when it pushes God out of our hearts.

The rest of the people turned violent, attacking the king's messengers, insulting them, and killing them. This pointed to the fierce persecution that Jewish leaders brought against God's prophets and Christian preachers. People who hate God often direct their anger at the ministers who deliver his word.

The king was filled with anger and sent his soldiers to wipe out those murderers and burn down their city. This was a prophecy about the Roman army destroying Jerusalem about forty years later. God used that event to bring judgment on those who killed his Son and rejected the gospel.

The king explained that the banquet was completely ready, but the original guests were not worthy to sit at his table. They proved they were unworthy because they treated his kind invitation with contempt. By despising his mercy, they lost all the blessings that had been prepared for them.

The king commanded his servants to go out to the busy street corners and invite every person they could find. This pictures the gospel moving outward from the Jewish leaders to the Gentiles and outcasts. God freely offers his salvation to anyone and everyone who will listen.

The servants obeyed and brought in all kinds of people from the streets, both bad and good, until the dining hall was full. The visible church on earth gathers all sorts of people, whether they were morally upright or open sinners before they heard the call. God's grace reaches out to gather a great family into his banquet.

When the king came in to greet the crowd, he noticed a man who was not wearing wedding clothes. In eastern royal banquets, appropriate robes were provided for the guests, so showing up in dirty street clothes was an insult to the host. This shows that God looks into his visible church and searches every heart to see if a person has truly been changed.

differ.view: The wedding garment means the perfect righteousness of Jesus credited to the believer, rather than good works or human effort.
The wedding garment represents the righteousness of Christ given to us and worked out as real personal holiness in our daily lives.
The wedding garment means true inward and outward holiness, which Christ gives to anyone who sincerely trusts him.

notes.meaning: The king asked the man how he dared to enter without proper wedding clothes, and the man had nothing to say. Calling him 'Friend' was a cold greeting that showed he had only pretended to belong to the king. When people stand before God, those who try to claim his blessings without true faith will have no excuse.

The king told his attendants to tie the man up and throw him out into the dark night. Outside the brightly lit wedding hall was a gloomy place where people wept and ground their teeth in misery. This shows the final judgment of hell, where those who only pretended to follow God are cut off from his joy forever.

Jesus concluded by stating that many are called, but few are chosen. A great number of people hear the outward message of the gospel, but not everyone truly welcomes it. Only those who respond with real faith and receive God's clothing will share in his eternal kingdom.

differ.view: The outward invitation goes to all people, but only those whom God has chosen by his grace are given the power to believe and enter life.
Many hear the gospel message, but only the few who choose to believe and seek God's gift of holiness are counted among the chosen.
God genuinely desires to save people, but he turns away those who refuse to let his grace make them fit for his kingdom.

notes.meaning: The Pharisees gathered in secret to plot how they could trap Jesus with his own words. Since they could not overpower his teaching openly, they tried to catch him with a tricky question. They hoped to force him into a mistake so they could hand him over to the authorities.

The Pharisees sent their students along with the Herodians, a political group that supported Roman rule, to speak with Jesus. They started with heavy flattery, calling him an honest teacher who was not afraid of any human being. They spoke these true words with false hearts, hoping he would speak recklessly without thinking.

They asked Jesus if God's law permitted Jews to pay the poll tax to the Roman emperor Caesar. This was a clever trap designed to ruin him no matter what he said. If he said yes, the Jewish crowd would call him a traitor to God; if he said no, the Herodians would report him to Rome for rebellion.

Jesus saw right through their evil plan and called them hypocrites, which means actors wearing a mask. Because he knows the human heart, their flattering words could not fool him. He openly exposed them for trying to trap him under the guise of an honest religious question.

Jesus told them to show him the silver coin used to pay the tax, and they brought him a denarius. The fact that they carried and used Roman money proved that they already accepted Roman government in their daily trade. Their own pockets held the evidence that ruined their argument.

Looking at the coin, Jesus asked whose portrait was carved on it and whose name was written there. The coin bore the likeness and official titles of the Roman emperor. By asking this, Jesus guided them to speak the simple fact that would break their trap.

When they replied that it was Caesar's coin, Jesus commanded them to give back to Caesar what belongs to him, and give to God what belongs to God. People should pay their taxes and obey earthly governments in civil matters. At the same time, because human souls bear God's image, our deepest love, worship, and obedience belong entirely to God.

When the messengers heard his answer, they were completely astonished and walked away in silence. His wisdom had answered their question fairly while completely destroying their trap. Even though they were amazed by his words, their hearts remained unchanged and they refused to follow him.

Later that same day, the Sadducees came to question Jesus. They were a wealthy group of religious leaders who claimed that the dead will never rise again, and they rejected the idea of spirits or a life after death. Although they usually argued with the Pharisees, both groups took turns trying to discredit Jesus.
